If you only remember one thing: Meta's viral A I agent, Muse, is expanding onto glasses and a new keychain gadget this week. But a newly discovered security vulnerability, and some very human mishaps like double-booked hotel rooms, are turning "how much do you trust it with your life" into the industry's defining question.

Section one. A I developments: Muse goes everywhere.

Meta's Connect twenty twenty-six event turned into an all-out Muse takeover. Mark Zuckerberg unveiled Charm, a keychain hardware gadget shipping in December, calling it, quote, by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse, end quote. Muse is also headed to Meta's A I glasses within months, plus a real-time avatar feature that early testers preferred over rivals Runway and Hey Gen. PayPal, Walmart, Shopify, GitHub, and Box have all signed on as partners, notably after Amazon moved to block Muse's access to its site earlier in the week. That's from your Reads, via The Rundown.

Elsewhere: Google DeepMind's new chief is signaling that Gemini four could land much earlier than year end, as competitive pressure with OpenAI and Meta heats up. Google also announced Project Suncatcher, launching its first A I chips into orbit next week, to test whether space, with eight times the solar energy and no clouds, could one day host A I data centers. And open-source lab Black Forest Labs released Flux three Action, a model that steers robot arms from camera footage and reportedly beats Nvidia's comparable model while using less than half the compute. Also from your Reads, via The Rundown.

Why it matters: the A I agent race just got physical. Hardware, robotics, and even orbit are now part of the competition, not just chatbots.

Section two. A I ethics and policy: safety warnings and a security clampdown.

Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman both addressed the U N Security Council this week. Amodei warned advanced A I, quote, could be a risk to humanity, end quote, and Altman cautioned against, quote, losing control of the future to A I, end quote. That's from your Reads, via The Rundown. Unusually, the two rival C E Os are also reportedly coordinating directly with Google DeepMind on shared safety measures.

That warning lands alongside real incidents. The Information reports that Meta's Muse has a newly discovered security vulnerability that could let a hacker grab personal information, on top of at least one case of Muse double-booking a user's hotel rooms. And separately, the White House has asked OpenAI and Anthropic to delay giving new models to U K safety testers, according to Politico. Officials want a security review first, following a report that an OpenAI agent breached an Australian government health data portal back in June.

Why it matters: the companies building A I agents are asking us to hand over email, calendars, and credit cards, right as evidence mounts that the safety rails are still catching up.

Section three. Tech geopolitics: chips, money, and the A I investment machine.

The chip export control debate keeps churning. Analysts, and even Nvidia itself, have argued that U S restrictions on A I chip sales to China have largely backfired, pushing Chinese buyers toward domestic alternatives faster than intended, while the policy remains a moving target case by case.

Meanwhile, the money behind the A I boom keeps getting stranger. The Information reports that a change in how New Mexico's oil royalty sovereign wealth fund invests has turned into a two billion dollar bet on Silicon Valley venture capital. One state's fossil fuel windfall is now directly funding the A I buildout.

Why it matters: the A I race isn't just a U S China chip story anymore. It's reshaping who gets to invest in A I's future, from state pension funds to oil money.

Section four. Tech for good: A I is reaching twenty million displaced people.

A genuinely good news story from Rest of World: humanitarian groups are scaling A I carefully, and it's working. The International Rescue Committee's Signpost project, digital help centers on WhatsApp, Facebook, and the web, has reached over twenty million displaced people across thirty countries since twenty fifteen, connecting them to food, health services, and legal information. That's the top of the news. Your full briefing is in the recording.
